data.content_ref: inline:The target's claim that preference is 'not a pragmatic gamble on success' directly contradicts the problem's requirement to explain why scientists 'prefer the better-corroborated theory' for action (e.g., building bridges). If the preference is merely to 'keep the engine running' without any expectation that the surviving theory is more reliable or likely to succeed in future applications than an untested one, then acting on it (choosing it for critical infrastructure) becomes irrational. Popper himself admitted we must act on the best-tested theory because it is the most rational choice; if this choice implies no pragmatic advantage or increased reliability (no 'gamble on success'), the target fails to explain the defensibility of the preference, leaving the charge of smuggled induction intact.
